screens.title: Deep Dive into systemd Initialization
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a mental model of how modern Linux systems start and reach a working state under systemd. You will learn why systemd runs as PID one, how it uses unit files and targets to describe system states, and how dependency directives drive parallel startup. Understanding this flow is essential for predictable server operations—especially when services depend on network, storage, or other system resources. We'll connect that model to practical tools: systemctl for inspection and control, and journalctl for root-cause analysis. For example, when a web service won’t start, the logs and dependency tree often reveal whether the issue is a missing mount, an unavailable network target, or a configuration error. By the end you will not only read unit files but reason about ordering, choose between Wants and Requires, and use daemon-reload safely. Keep in mind a common misconception: systemd is not just a replacement for init scripts; it is a coordinated service manager with strong dependency semantics. Ready to explore targets, units, commands, and a short lab to create a network-dependent service?

screens.title: What systemd is and why PID 1 matters
screens.narratorSegment: Systemd is the init system and service manager that takes control as PID one when the kernel finishes booting. As PID one, systemd inherits special responsibilities: it is the ultimate parent process, it reaps zombies, and it decides which units to activate to reach the system's desired state. This central position gives systemd power to orchestrate the entire boot sequence, but it also means misconfiguration at this layer can affect the whole host. A concrete example: if default. target points to multi-user. target and a required mount unit fails, the system may stop before reaching a usable multi-user environment. A common misconception is thinking systemd only runs scripts in order; instead it resolves dependencies and runs units in parallel whenever safe, using directives for ordering and necessity. Knowing PID one’s role helps you understand why you must carefully use Requires= versus Wants= and why testing changes with daemon-reload and controlled restart is important. Takeaway: think of systemd as a directed graph manager with PID one coordinating nodes—your edits change the graph, so choose directives that reflect true criticality. What systemd is and why PID 1 matters means systemd runs as pid 1 and orchestrates system startup by managing units and dependencies; mistakes here have system-wide impact.. In practical terms, define systemd, its role as pid 1, and the implications for system management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What systemd is and why PID 1 matters
Core Concept
systemd as PID 1
systemd becomes the first userland process after the kernel boots, responsible for bringing the machine to the configured target by reading unit files and resolving dependencies. Because it is PID 1, it has unique process-management responsibilities and broad control over service lifecycle.
Why it matters
Errors at PID 1 level affect all services. Use careful dependency choices and test unit changes in a safe environment.
Misconception
systemd is not just sequential scripts; it builds and executes a dependency graph with parallel activation where possible.
Analogy
Think of systemd as a conductor for an orchestra. Each unit is an instrument; PID 1 signals when each should start so the full performance reaches the intended state on time.
Key Takeaway
Treat PID one configuration changes with caution. Use safe testing and backups before editing unit files that affect boot.

screens.title: systemd Boot Flow: kernel → systemd → target
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the boot flow so you can visualize how the kernel boots the system and hands control to systemd, which then activates targets and units. First, the kernel finishes initialization and executes the systemd binary as PID one. systemd reads its configuration and unit directories, then resolves default. target. default. target typically aliases to multi-user. target or graphical. target. Next, systemd evaluates the dependency graph: it finds all units required or wanted by the target and orders them based on After and Before directives while launching non-dependent units in parallel. For example, multi-user. target will pull in network and storage units if they are listed; graphical. target includes display manager units in addition to multi-user. target. If a critical dependency is marked with Requires= and it fails, systemd marks the dependent unit as failed as well, potentially preventing the target from being reached. A common mistake is assuming services start sequentially; the parallel model improves speed but requires careful dependency definitions. Takeaway: think of boot as graph resolution with parallel execution constrained by ordering and requirement directives. What initial failures would you check first when a system doesn’t reach multi-user. target? Answer: required mounts and network targets.

keyIdea.text: systemd resolves default.target, builds a dependency graph, and activates units in parallel constrained by ordering and requirement directives.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › systemd Boot Flow
Process Flow
kernel → systemd → default.target → units
1. Kernel executes systemd as PID 1. systemd becomes the first userland process with special responsibilities.
2. systemd reads unit directories and resolves default.target, typically an alias to multi-user.target or graphical.target.
3. systemd builds the dependency graph and activates units in parallel where possible, honoring After/Before ordering.
4. If a required unit fails, dependent units may fail and the system may not reach the target; check required mounts and network targets first.
Example
When default.target points to multi-user.target, and multi-user.target requires a network mount that fails, services needing network will not start. Use list-dependencies to trace which unit failed first.
Common Mistake
Using Requires= for non-critical services causes cascading failures. Prefer Wants= for softer dependencies when appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Boot is dependency resolution plus parallel activation. Troubleshoot by finding the first failed required unit.

screens.title: Unit types and file locations
screens.narratorSegment: Unit files are simple text files that tell systemd how to manage a resource. The common types you'll use as an LFCE candidate include service for daemons, socket for sockets or IPC activation, mount and automount for filesystems, target for grouping units, timer for scheduled tasks, path for file-system triggers, device for kernel devices, and slice for resource control. Unit files live in three primary locations: /etc/systemd/system for administrator overrides and custom units, /run/systemd/system for runtime-generated units, and /usr/lib/systemd/system for packaged, vendor-provided units. systemd searches these directories in that order so local changes in /etc take precedence. A concrete example: to override a packaged webserver unit, copy its file from /usr/lib/systemd/system into /etc/systemd/system and edit it. Don’t forget to run systemctl daemon-reload to apply changes. A frequent misconception is editing a file under /usr/lib directly; such edits may be overwritten by package updates. Instead, prefer overrides in /etc and document the change. Understanding types and locations lets you manage custom services safely and predictably. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Unit types and file locations
Definition
Unit types you will use
  • service: daemon management and process supervision.
  • socket: socket-based activation for services on demand.
  • mount / automount: filesystem mounts and on-demand mounts.
  • target: groups other units to represent system states.
  • timer / path: scheduled tasks and filesystem event triggers.
File locations
systemd searches these locations in order: /etc/systemd/system for local overrides, /run/systemd/system for runtime units, and /usr/lib/systemd/system for vendor units. Local admin changes should go to /etc.
Practical example
Copy a packaged unit from /usr/lib/systemd/system into /etc/systemd/system to override it, then run systemctl daemon-reload and restart the unit to apply changes.
Misconception
Editing vendor files in /usr/lib directly is unsafe because package upgrades may overwrite changes. Use /etc overrides and document adjustments.

screens.title: Advanced systemctl commands
screens.narratorSegment: systemctl is your primary control surface for interacting with systemd. Beyond start and stop, several commands reveal deep unit state. Use systemctl status unit to get a quick overview, including a condensed log excerpt. Use systemctl show unit to get all properties as key-value pairs—this helps when you need environment variables, ExecStart paths, or restart settings. For dependency analysis, systemctl list-dependencies unit reveals the whole tree of Wants and Requires, which is crucial for tracing failures. For quick checks, systemctl is-active and systemctl is-enabled tell you runtime state and whether a unit is configured to start at boot. After editing unit files, always run systemctl daemon-reload; without it systemd will not pick up changed files. A concrete example: if a service fails, run systemctl status to see the last messages, then run journalctl -u to inspect full logs, and use list-dependencies to find an upstream required unit that failed first. A common mistake is editing a file and starting the unit without daemon-reload, which leaves systemd using the old configuration. Practice these commands until they become an efficient diagnostic pattern.

keyIdea.text: Use status, show, list-dependencies, is-active/is-enabled, and daemon-reload together to inspect and apply unit changes safely.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Advanced systemctl commands
Command Patterns
systemctl status <unit> — quick state and recent logs.
systemctl show <unit> — full property dump for debugging options and paths.
systemctl list-dependencies <unit> — dependency tree to trace upstream failures.
systemctl is-active / is-enabled <unit> — quick checks for runtime and boot-time configuration.
systemctl daemon-reload — informs systemd of unit file changes; run after edits.
Example Debug Session
sudo systemctl status mywebapp.service
sudo journalctl -u mywebapp.service --since "10 minutes ago"
sudo systemctl list-dependencies mywebapp.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart mywebapp.service
Common Mistake
Skipping daemon-reload after editing unit files leaves systemd running old definitions, producing confusing behavior.
Key Takeaway

Combine status, journalctl, and list-dependencies to find the first failing unit, then apply safe edits and run daemon-reload.

screens.title: Dependency directives: Requires vs Wants, After vs Before
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency directives are how unit files express relationships. Requires= denotes a strong dependency: if the required unit fails to activate, the unit with Requires= will also fail. Wants= is weaker: systemd will try to start the wanted unit, but its failure does not force the dependent unit to fail. For ordering, After= and Before= only affect the order of activation; they do not create a requirement unless paired with Requires= or Wants=. A practical example: use After=network-online. target to ensure your service starts after network is configured; pair it with Wants=network-online. target if you want systemd to attempt to bring the network up but not fail your service if the network target does not come online. A common trap is using Requires= for a non-critical component, which creates cascading failures when that component has intermittent issues. When in doubt, prefer Wants= for services that can tolerate absence. Another pitfall is forgetting that After= only orders activation—it does not wait for full readiness unless the other unit properly signals readiness. Takeaway: choose Requires for true critical dependency, Wants for softer dependencies, and use ordering directives to control start sequence.

keyIdea.title: Dependency semantics
keyIdea.text: Requires/Wants control necessity; After/Before control ordering. Use the correct combination to avoid cascading failures.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Dependency directives
Necessity
Requires= vs Wants=

Requires= creates a strong requirement. If the required unit fails, the requiring unit also fails.

Wants= is weaker. systemd will attempt to start the wanted unit, but its failure does not force the other unit to fail.

Ordering
After= / Before=

After= and Before= set activation order but do not by themselves create a dependency. Pair ordering with Requires or Wants when you also need the service started.

Concrete Example
A web app should use After=network-online.target and Wants=network-online.target. This orders the web app to start after the network target and asks systemd to bring the network target up, without making the web app fail if the network target does not come online.
Common Mistake
Using Requires= for non-critical components creates unnecessary cascading failures. Reserve Requires= for true system-critical dependencies.

screens.title: Troubleshooting startup failures with journalctl
screens.narratorSegment: Journalctl centralizes systemd logs and is the first place to look when a service fails at boot or runtime. Start by running journalctl -u to see all messages for a unit, or journalctl -b to view logs from the current boot. When diagnosing a failed unit, your goal is to find the initial failure, not the last symptom. For example, if mywebapp. service shows failed, check journalctl -u mywebapp. service --since "10 minutes ago" to inspect timestamps and repeated restart attempts. Then use systemctl list-dependencies to see upstream units that may have failed earlier. Remember that systemd often retries services; you may see multiple failure entries. Look for the first non-successful exit or the first error mentioning a missing mount, network issue, or permission problem. A common misconception is assuming the service log contains all context; sometimes the dependent unit's logs show the root cause. Final step: after identifying the issue, fix the configuration, run daemon-reload if you changed unit files, and restart the service while tailing logs to verify resolution. Question to reflect on: which upstream component would you check first if a database-dependent web service won’t start?

keyIdea.text: Use journalctl to locate the first failing event; combine with systemctl list-dependencies to trace upstream causes and iterate fixes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Troubleshooting with journalctl
Process
Find the first failure and trace upstream
  1. Run journalctl -u <unit> to see unit logs and timestamps.
  2. Use journalctl -b to view current boot logs for context.
  3. Check systemctl list-dependencies <unit> to find upstream units to inspect.
  4. Fix the root cause, run daemon-reload if needed, and restart while following logs live.
Example commands
sudo journalctl -u mywebapp.service --since "10 minutes ago"
sudo journalctl -b | less
sudo systemctl list-dependencies mywebapp.service
Pitfall
Reading only recent messages can mislead you; always look back to the first error occurrence to avoid chasing the symptom.
Key Takeaway

Journalctl is indispensable. Use it to find the initial error and pair it with dependency tracing to locate the root cause.

screens.title: Create a custom service: server script and unit file

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Create a custom service
Server Script
A minimal Python server placed at /opt/mywebapp/server.py. It serves files on port 8000 and lets systemd capture logs.
# content excerpt
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import http.server
import socketserver
PORT = 8000
DIRECTORY = "/opt/mywebapp"
# Handler serves DIRECTORY and suppresses stdout logging
with socketserver.TCPServer(("", PORT), http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler) as httpd:
  httpd.serve_forever()
Unit File
Place this file at /etc/systemd/system/mywebapp.service and then reload systemd.
[Unit]
Description=My Simple Python Web Application
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=nobody
Group=nogroup
ExecStart=/opt/mywebapp/server.py
WorkingDirectory=/opt/mywebapp
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Key Takeaway

After creating the files, run daemon-reload, enable, and start the unit. Verify with systemctl status, journalctl -u, and curl to confirm service availability.

screens.title: Unit lifecycle and restart policies
screens.narratorSegment: Restart policies govern how systemd responds to service exits and are critical for resilient services. The Restart= directive accepts several modes, and the example uses Restart=on-failure, which restarts the unit when the process exits with a non-zero status or is terminated by a signal. This is a sensible default for many application services that should recover from transient errors. For aggressive recovery, systemd also supports Restart=always; for conservative behavior, Restart=no disables automatic restarts. RestartSec defines how long systemd waits before attempting a restart; setting RestartSec=5s prevents rapid restart loops that can waste resources. A common pitfall is enabling Restart=always without limits when a service consistently fails—this may trigger frequent restarts and overload logs. To manage such scenarios, combine RestartWithExitStatus checks or use StartLimitInterval and StartLimitBurst settings to protect the system. Practical example: for a web server that binds to a port, use Restart=on-failure to recover from crashes, but monitor logs to ensure the underlying problem isn't persistent. Takeaway: choose a restart mode matching your service criticality and add rate-limiting to avoid noisy loops. Unit lifecycle and restart policies means restart=on-failure and restartsec balance resilience with safety; use restart limits to avoid runaway restart loops.. In practical terms, understanding restart= modes and restartsec to manage service resilience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Unit lifecycle and restart policies
Restart policies
Manage resilience and safety
  • Restart=on-failure: restarts on non-zero exits or signals.
  • Restart=always: restarts regardless of exit status.
  • Restart=no: do not restart automatically.
  • RestartSec= delays before retry to avoid tight loops.
Rate limiting
Use StartLimitInterval and StartLimitBurst to prevent repeated restarts from overwhelming the host if a service keeps failing.
StartLimitInterval=10s
StartLimitBurst=5
Practical Example
For mywebapp.service, Restart=on-failure and RestartSec=5s gives automated recovery while avoiding log floods. Combine with monitoring to fix recurring root causes.

screens.title: Safe editing workflow and daemon-reload
screens.narratorSegment: When managing unit files in production, adopt a cautious workflow. First, back up any original unit file before editing. Prefer creating an override in /etc/systemd/system rather than modifying vendor files under /usr/lib. After making changes, run systemctl daemon-reload so systemd becomes aware of the new or changed unit definitions. Next, test changes with systemctl start or restart and verify using systemctl status and journalctl -u. If the unit should persist across boots, run systemctl enable so it will be started by WantedBy targets like multi-user. target. A typical mistake is enabling a broken unit without testing it, which can cause boot-time failures. For critical hosts, perform changes in a maintenance window or controlled environment and document the modification. Example: copy /usr/lib/systemd/system/myapp. service to /etc/systemd/system/myapp. service. d/override. conf or edit the copy, daemon-reload, and then restart. Finally, use systemctl is-enabled and is-active to confirm configuration and runtime state before exiting your maintenance session. These steps reduce the risk of leaving a system unbootable. Safe editing workflow and daemon-reload means back up vendor units, place overrides in /etc, run daemon-reload, test with start/status, then enable for boot persistence when safe.. In practical terms, best practices: backups, overrides, daemon-reload, and enabling services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Safe editing workflow
Checklist
  1. Back up original unit files before modifications.
  2. Prefer /etc overrides rather than editing /usr/lib directly.
  3. Run systemctl daemon-reload after changes.
  4. Test with start/restart and verify with status and journalctl.
  5. Enable only after successful verification if persistent boot behavior is desired.
Example Commands
sudo cp /usr/lib/systemd/system/myapp.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart myapp.service
sudo systemctl status myapp.service
sudo systemctl enable myapp.service
Practical Tip
Test changes in a non-production environment, validate with logs, and keep a copy of the original unit to recover quickly if needed.

screens.title: Assessment scenarios & common troubleshooting questions
screens.narratorSegment: To solidify understanding, let's run through two assessment scenarios that mirror real troubleshooting tasks. Scenario one: your custom mycustomapp. service must start only after full network connectivity and must restart on failure. Which directives do you choose? The correct pattern uses After=network-online. target and Wants=network-online. target in the [Unit] section to order and request network readiness, and Restart=on-failure in [Service] to recover from crashes. Consider why Requires= might be too strict: if the network target fails intermittently, Requires= could cause your unit to fail and prevent reaching the target. Scenario two: postgres. service shows failed. systemctl status shows a failed state. What do you run next? First run journalctl -u postgres. service --since "1 hour ago" to capture recent logs and find the initial error messages. Then run systemctl list-dependencies postgres. service to inspect upstream requirements like mounts or network targets. Explain why journalctl is effective: it centralizes unit logs including start attempts and error traces so you can pinpoint the first failing component. These tasks require both command fluency and cause-effect reasoning—practice each until you can quickly find the initial failure in a chain.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Assessment Scenarios
Question 1
Network-dependent service must start after network and restart on failure
Correct directives: After=network-online.target and Wants=network-online.target in [Unit], and Restart=on-failure in [Service]. Requires= is too strong for many applications and can cause cascading failures.
Question 2
Database service shows failed—what do you run next?
Run journalctl -u postgres.service --since "1 hour ago" to see logs and find the initial failure. Then inspect systemctl list-dependencies postgres.service to find an upstream failing unit like a mount or network target.
Key Takeaway

Answering these questions requires both command knowledge and causal tracing. Focus on identifying the first failure, not the final symptom.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to keep front of mind. First, systemd runs as PID one and orchestrates system startup by reading unit files and resolving dependencies. Second, unit files come in several types—service, socket, mount, target, timer—and you should use /etc for overrides so changes persist safely. Third, dependency directives like Requires, Wants, After, and Before determine necessity and ordering; choose Requires only for true critical dependencies and prefer Wants for softer ties. Fourth, systemctl and journalctl form a diagnostic pair: systemctl exposes unit state and dependency trees while journalctl provides the logs needed to find the initial failure. Finally, adopt safe workflows—back up unit files, daemon-reload after edits, test, and enable only after validation. Keep practicing with the hands-on example to make these ideas second nature. Which dependency would you check first when a multi-service system fails to reach its target? That question should guide your initial investigation.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: These three compact reminders will serve you daily. First, always treat systemd configuration as graph changes: your unit edits modify relationships that determine startup order and success. Second, use the correct directory for edits—/etc/systemd/system for overrides—then run systemctl daemon-reload to apply changes; skipping this step is a frequent source of confusion. Third, pair systemctl commands with journalctl when troubleshooting: status and list-dependencies show state and relationships, while journalctl -u shows chronology and the initial error. If you remember these three rules—think in graphs, use /etc with daemon-reload, and pair systemctl with journalctl—you will dramatically reduce the time you spend diagnosing startup problems. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a mental model of how modern Linux systems start and reach a working state under systemd. You will learn why systemd runs as PID one, how it uses unit files and targets to describe system states, and how dependency directives drive parallel startup. Understanding this flow is essential for predictable server operations—especially when services depend on network, storage, or other system resources. We'll connect that model to practical tools: systemctl for inspection and control, and journalctl for root-cause analysis. For example, when a web service won’t start, the logs and dependency tree often reveal whether the issue is a missing mount, an unavailable network target, or a configuration error. By the end you will not only read unit files but reason about ordering, choose between Wants and Requires, and use daemon-reload safely. Keep in mind a common misconception: systemd is not just a replacement for init scripts; it is a coordinated service manager with strong dependency semantics. Ready to explore targets, units, commands, and a short lab to create a network-dependent service?

These learning objectives map to the skills you'll practice and verify. First, you'll be able to explain the systemd boot flow, including how the kernel passes control to systemd as PID one and how targets drive system state. This matters because reasoning about boot order helps you avoid services blocking system startup. Second, you'll analyze and interpret unit files for services, targets, and mounts, so you can customize behavior and adjust dependencies. That skill prevents misconfiguration errors that often make services fail silently. Third, you'll use advanced systemctl commands—status, show, list-dependencies, daemon-reload—to inspect and manage units in a live system. These commands are essential for efficient diagnostics in production. Finally, you'll troubleshoot startup issues using journalctl and dependency tracing, learning to find the initial failure and fix it safely. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with commands you can run, and each milestone includes a verification step to prove competency.

This second objectives slide focuses on application and verification in real scenarios. You'll practice creating unit files that align with dependency patterns and apply Restart policies safely. For instance, you'll create a simple web server unit that uses After=network-online. target and Restart=on-failure so it waits for network availability and recovers from crashes. You will also practice using systemctl daemon-reload after editing unit files, because without a reload systemd won’t pick up changes. In troubleshooting exercises you will combine systemctl status, journalctl -u, and list-dependencies to find the initial point of failure. This approach helps you avoid a common trap: interpreting only the last failure instead of the first failure in the chain. Finally, you'll learn safe testing habits, such as backing up unit files and testing changes in a controlled environment to avoid rendering a host unbootable. Each objective is tied to a verification milestone so you can confirm competency.

Systemd is the init system and service manager that takes control as PID one when the kernel finishes booting. As PID one, systemd inherits special responsibilities: it is the ultimate parent process, it reaps zombies, and it decides which units to activate to reach the system's desired state. This central position gives systemd power to orchestrate the entire boot sequence, but it also means misconfiguration at this layer can affect the whole host. A concrete example: if default. target points to multi-user. target and a required mount unit fails, the system may stop before reaching a usable multi-user environment. A common misconception is thinking systemd only runs scripts in order; instead it resolves dependencies and runs units in parallel whenever safe, using directives for ordering and necessity. Knowing PID one’s role helps you understand why you must carefully use Requires= versus Wants= and why testing changes with daemon-reload and controlled restart is important. Takeaway: think of systemd as a directed graph manager with PID one coordinating nodes—your edits change the graph, so choose directives that reflect true criticality. What systemd is and why PID 1 matters means systemd runs as pid 1 and orchestrates system startup by managing units and dependencies; mistakes here have system-wide impact.. In practical terms, define systemd, its role as pid 1, and the implications for system management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the boot flow so you can visualize how the kernel boots the system and hands control to systemd, which then activates targets and units. First, the kernel finishes initialization and executes the systemd binary as PID one. systemd reads its configuration and unit directories, then resolves default. target. default. target typically aliases to multi-user. target or graphical. target. Next, systemd evaluates the dependency graph: it finds all units required or wanted by the target and orders them based on After and Before directives while launching non-dependent units in parallel. For example, multi-user. target will pull in network and storage units if they are listed; graphical. target includes display manager units in addition to multi-user. target. If a critical dependency is marked with Requires= and it fails, systemd marks the dependent unit as failed as well, potentially preventing the target from being reached. A common mistake is assuming services start sequentially; the parallel model improves speed but requires careful dependency definitions. Takeaway: think of boot as graph resolution with parallel execution constrained by ordering and requirement directives. What initial failures would you check first when a system doesn’t reach multi-user. target? Answer: required mounts and network targets.

Unit files are simple text files that tell systemd how to manage a resource. The common types you'll use as an LFCE candidate include service for daemons, socket for sockets or IPC activation, mount and automount for filesystems, target for grouping units, timer for scheduled tasks, path for file-system triggers, device for kernel devices, and slice for resource control. Unit files live in three primary locations: /etc/systemd/system for administrator overrides and custom units, /run/systemd/system for runtime-generated units, and /usr/lib/systemd/system for packaged, vendor-provided units. systemd searches these directories in that order so local changes in /etc take precedence. A concrete example: to override a packaged webserver unit, copy its file from /usr/lib/systemd/system into /etc/systemd/system and edit it. Don’t forget to run systemctl daemon-reload to apply changes. A frequent misconception is editing a file under /usr/lib directly; such edits may be overwritten by package updates. Instead, prefer overrides in /etc and document the change. Understanding types and locations lets you manage custom services safely and predictably. Unit types and file locations means unit files declare resource behavior; key types include service, socket, mount, target, and timer. use /etc for overrides and run daemon-reload after changes.. In practical terms, service, socket, mount, target, timer, and where unit files live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

systemctl is your primary control surface for interacting with systemd. Beyond start and stop, several commands reveal deep unit state. Use systemctl status unit to get a quick overview, including a condensed log excerpt. Use systemctl show unit to get all properties as key-value pairs—this helps when you need environment variables, ExecStart paths, or restart settings. For dependency analysis, systemctl list-dependencies unit reveals the whole tree of Wants and Requires, which is crucial for tracing failures. For quick checks, systemctl is-active and systemctl is-enabled tell you runtime state and whether a unit is configured to start at boot. After editing unit files, always run systemctl daemon-reload; without it systemd will not pick up changed files. A concrete example: if a service fails, run systemctl status to see the last messages, then run journalctl -u to inspect full logs, and use list-dependencies to find an upstream required unit that failed first. A common mistake is editing a file and starting the unit without daemon-reload, which leaves systemd using the old configuration. Practice these commands until they become an efficient diagnostic pattern.

Dependency directives are how unit files express relationships. Requires= denotes a strong dependency: if the required unit fails to activate, the unit with Requires= will also fail. Wants= is weaker: systemd will try to start the wanted unit, but its failure does not force the dependent unit to fail. For ordering, After= and Before= only affect the order of activation; they do not create a requirement unless paired with Requires= or Wants=. A practical example: use After=network-online. target to ensure your service starts after network is configured; pair it with Wants=network-online. target if you want systemd to attempt to bring the network up but not fail your service if the network target does not come online. A common trap is using Requires= for a non-critical component, which creates cascading failures when that component has intermittent issues. When in doubt, prefer Wants= for services that can tolerate absence. Another pitfall is forgetting that After= only orders activation—it does not wait for full readiness unless the other unit properly signals readiness. Takeaway: choose Requires for true critical dependency, Wants for softer dependencies, and use ordering directives to control start sequence.

Journalctl centralizes systemd logs and is the first place to look when a service fails at boot or runtime. Start by running journalctl -u to see all messages for a unit, or journalctl -b to view logs from the current boot. When diagnosing a failed unit, your goal is to find the initial failure, not the last symptom. For example, if mywebapp. service shows failed, check journalctl -u mywebapp. service --since "10 minutes ago" to inspect timestamps and repeated restart attempts. Then use systemctl list-dependencies to see upstream units that may have failed earlier. Remember that systemd often retries services; you may see multiple failure entries. Look for the first non-successful exit or the first error mentioning a missing mount, network issue, or permission problem. A common misconception is assuming the service log contains all context; sometimes the dependent unit's logs show the root cause. Final step: after identifying the issue, fix the configuration, run daemon-reload if you changed unit files, and restart the service while tailing logs to verify resolution. Restart policies govern how systemd responds to service exits and are critical for resilient services. The Restart= directive accepts several modes, and the example uses Restart=on-failure, which restarts the unit when the process exits with a non-zero status or is terminated by a signal. This is a sensible default for many application services that should recover from transient errors. For aggressive recovery, systemd also supports Restart=always; for conservative behavior, Restart=no disables automatic restarts. RestartSec defines how long systemd waits before attempting a restart; setting RestartSec=5s prevents rapid restart loops that can waste resources. A common pitfall is enabling Restart=always without limits when a service consistently fails—this may trigger frequent restarts and overload logs. To manage such scenarios, combine RestartWithExitStatus checks or use StartLimitInterval and StartLimitBurst settings to protect the system. When managing unit files in production, adopt a cautious workflow. First, back up any original unit file before editing. Prefer creating an override in /etc/systemd/system rather than modifying vendor files under /usr/lib. After making changes, run systemctl daemon-reload so systemd becomes aware of the new or changed unit definitions. Next, test changes with systemctl start or restart and verify using systemctl status and journalctl -u. If the unit should persist across boots, run systemctl enable so it will be started by WantedBy targets like multi-user. target. A typical mistake is enabling a broken unit without testing it, which can cause boot-time failures. For critical hosts, perform changes in a maintenance window or controlled environment and document the modification. Finally, use systemctl is-enabled and is-active to confirm configuration and runtime state before exiting your maintenance session. These steps reduce the risk of leaving a system unbootable. Let's summarize the essential concepts to keep front of mind. First, systemd runs as PID one and orchestrates system startup by reading unit files and resolving dependencies. Third, dependency directives like Requires, Wants, After, and Before determine necessity and ordering; choose Requires only for true critical dependencies and prefer Wants for softer ties.
